title: Americans view U.S. global power through sharply partisan lenses, with broad agreement that it interferes abroad
source_unit: Pew Research Center, Most Americans Now Say U.S. Foreign Policy Ignores the Interests of Other Countries, April 2026, based on the American Trends Panel
geography: United States; adults nationally with party, age, and global-country comparisons

observations.period: March 23-29, 2026; U.S. consideration of other countries' interests

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in Pew American Trends Panel Wave 190; survey response rate 87%

us_ignores_other_interests.unit: percent saying the U.S. considers other countries' interests not too much or not at all

democrats_see_ignoring.unit: reported share saying the U.S. ignores other countries' interests

republicans_see_consideration.value: at least two-thirds of Republicans have said the U.S. considers other countries' interests across the historical series

observations.method: Pew Research Center nationally representative American Trends Panel survey conducted March 23-29, 2026; online and live telephone interviews in English and Spanish, with historical comparisons from prior Pew waves.
observations.uncertainty: These are public perceptions of foreign-policy orientation, not coded policy behavior, diplomatic outcomes, partner responses, or an evaluation of whether U.S. decisions actually considered foreign interests.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults nationally, with Democratic and Republican comparisons and historical administration context.
observations.counterinterpretation: The partisan shift may reflect changes in administration, policy visibility, media framing, or partisan identity rather than a common public assessment of a stable foreign-policy doctrine.

observations.period: March 2026; perceived global role and partisan divergence

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the March 23-29, 2026 Pew survey

contributes_to_peace_total.unit: percent saying the U.S. contributes a great deal or fair amount to global peace and stability

us_respected_democrats.unit: percent of Democrats saying the U.S. is respected around the world

us_respected_republicans.unit: percent of Republicans saying the U.S. is respected around the world

observations.method: Pew survey comparison of perceived U.S. global standing by party, using common questions about peace, respect, foreign-policy consideration, influence, and interference.
observations.uncertainty: Partisan differences are associations in public opinion and do not establish differences in information, experience, ideology, or actual U.S. global performance; multiple perceptions may be held simultaneously.
observations.subgroup: Democrats and Republicans in the U.S. adult population.
observations.counterinterpretation: A respondent can believe the U.S. is powerful yet disrespectful, influential yet interventionist, or protective of peace while ignoring other countries' interests; the measures are not one-dimensional approval scales.

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the March 23-29, 2026 Pew survey; some country questions use a random half-sample

us_interferes_total.unit: percent saying the U.S. interferes in other countries' affairs a great deal or fair amount

influence_getting_weaker.unit: percent saying U.S. influence has been getting weaker in recent years

influence_getting_stronger.unit: percent saying U.S. influence has been getting stronger

republicans_influence_stronger.unit: percent among Republicans saying influence is getting stronger

observations.method: Pew repeated cross-sectional comparison of U.S. adults' views of interference and influence, including party and age splits.
observations.uncertainty: Perceived interference is not a coded count of interventions, and perceived influence is not a measure of military, economic, diplomatic, or cultural power; historical comparisons are subject to changing contexts and survey modes.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults nationally, with Democratic/Republican and age comparisons.
observations.counterinterpretation: Broad agreement that the U.S. interferes abroad can coexist with disagreement over whether that interference is legitimate, stabilizing, effective, or evidence of strength.

denominator.unit: U.S. adults receiving the open-ended country-ranking form

us_named_global_superpower.unit: percent naming the U.S. as a global superpower

china_named_global_superpower.unit: percent naming China as a global superpower

observations.method: Pew open-ended question asked a randomly selected half-sample which countries are militarily and economically dominant global superpowers; multiple answers were allowed.
observations.uncertainty: The measure captures public conceptions of superpower status, not a geopolitical index or expert assessment; open-ended recognition may reflect salience, familiarity, or current events.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults in the relevant random half-sample, with party comparisons reported in the source.
observations.counterinterpretation: Naming the U.S. as a superpower does not imply approval of U.S. policy, confidence in its legitimacy, or expectation that its influence is growing.

boundary: This record adds a US-to-world legitimacy layer: Americans' perceptions of U.S. power, respect, interference, peace contribution, and attention to other countries are strongly partisan and internally multidimensional. It does not establish actual foreign-policy conduct, diplomatic influence, partner trust, geopolitical outcomes, or causal effects of public opinion on policy.
